source: CARDI -- Soil Fertility Management for Rice Cultivation in Cambodia (2010)
text:
Cambodian rice soils can be identified and classified in the field without needing detailed maps or laboratory analysis -- a simple, low-cost method farmers and extension workers can use directly at the field.

Simple field texture test (the 'ribbon test'): take a small handful of soil, remove any stones, roots, or plant debris, then slowly moisten it with water while kneading it in your palm until it just starts to feel sticky. Judge the texture as follows: SANDY soil has little or no stickiness, feels gritty, and crumbles apart easily or forms only rough clumps with no smooth shape, often showing visible cracks and not feeling sticky. LOAMY soil can be rolled into a rope or ribbon shape (about 13cm long, 0.6cm thick) that does not stick firmly to the hand, can be bent into a U-shape or ring, shows some cracking when bent, and feels slightly slippery like soap, though it may still contain small amounts of grit. CLAY soil can be rolled into a smooth, sticky ribbon that clings to the palm, bends into a ring or curve without cracking, feels smooth and slippery like soap when wet, though it may still contain a few small grit particles.

Soil color: compare a moist soil sample against a standard soil color reference chart (used with 3-5 people comparing together, in bright natural light, without sunglasses) -- color depends on the base soil color plus any mottling (patches of a different color, which indicate drainage conditions).

Soil layer depth: dig a hole roughly 50cm deep and examine two layers -- the topsoil layer (0-20cm, the layer that gets plowed) and the subsoil layer (20-50cm below that).

Proper soil sampling for comparison: dig a pit roughly 0.5m x 0.5m x 0.5m (one pit is enough to represent about 1 hectare). Take 3 sub-samples per soil layer, mix them together, then compare the mixed sample against the soil color and texture reference guide, noting texture, color, presence of a hardpan layer, and presence of stones or gravel for each layer.

Why this matters: Cambodia has at least 11 major rice soil groups (including Prey Khmer, Prateah Lang, Bakan, Krakor, Toul Samnang, Kbal Po, Kean Svay, Kampong Siem, and others), each with very different fertility levels, water-holding capacity, and fertilizer response -- for example, Prey Khmer soil is sandy, low-fertility, and difficult to manage, while Krakor and Kbal Po soils are naturally more fertile with good response to nitrogen fertilizer. Identifying which soil group a field belongs to is the necessary first step before deciding on fertilizer type and amount, since the right fertilizer approach differs significantly by soil group.
